title: "Bayesian machine learning"
subtitle: "Lecture 14"

## Overview

By the end of this lecture you can place a prior directly on a regression function rather
than on a finite coefficient vector, and say how much of that function's shape the data
chose rather than the prior.

::: {.callout-important}
## The result of this chapter

For inputs $x$, let $k(x,x')$ be a kernel that is positive semidefinite for every finite
collection of inputs, and let $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0,k)$. Given training data $y = f(X) +
\varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n^2 I)$ and new inputs $X_*$, the
posterior over $f_* = f(X_*)$ is exactly Gaussian,

$$
f_* \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar m, \bar V), \qquad
\bar m = K_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} y, \qquad
\bar V = K_{**} - K_*^\top(K+\sigma_n^2 I)^{-1}K_*,
$$

for any number of training points, any number of new inputs, and any positive semidefinite
$k$. It replaces a point estimate of the function by a full distribution over it, at no
cost beyond a Cholesky factorisation, and the difficulty moves from choosing a coefficient
vector to choosing the kernel and its hyperparameters.
:::

After working through this chapter you can

1. diagnose why a model linear in the predictors is one particular choice of kernel;
2. derive the Gaussian process posterior mean and variance from a joint Normal identity;
3. derive the marginal likelihood of a Gaussian process as fit minus complexity;
4. implement squared-exponential Gaussian process regression in Python with no
   optimisation loop;
5. compare a Gaussian process against a Bayesian linear model out of sample by root mean
   squared error and by log predictive score;
6. interpret a flaring credible band as an honest admission of extrapolation, not a defect
   of the method.

Week 14 of 15, paired with the [Week 14 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/14-bayesian-machine-learning.qmd). The chapter assumes the
Normal linear regression posterior of Lecture 2 and the completing-the-square argument used
throughout the course; no sampler is needed, because conditioning a Gaussian process is
closed form.

## Motivation: a relationship no coefficient can bend {#sec-motivation}

Every model this course has built, from the single regression of Lecture 2 to the
portfolio weights of Lecture 13, wrote the conditional mean as a linear function of the
predictors, $E[y \mid x] = x^\top\beta$. Shrinkage changed how $\beta$ was estimated, the
state-space model let it move over time, and stochastic volatility let the variance move,
but in every case a fixed vector of coefficients decided how the outcome responds to each
predictor, and that response was a straight line. Nothing in the machinery so far ever
asked whether a straight line was the right shape.

The question this section puts to the machinery is a standard one for a macroeconomist:
how much will industrial production grow over the coming twelve months, given the shape of
the yield curve today? The term spread, the ten-year Treasury yield minus the federal
funds rate, is the classic leading indicator, and the theory behind it is not a straight
line. An inverted curve, spread below zero, is a recession signal and recessions cut
output hard. A curve that is already steep says policy is loose and recovery is under way,
but a curve twice as steep does not mean twice the recovery, because output cannot expand
without limit. The relationship should climb steeply out of inversion and then flatten,
which is a shape no coefficient can produce.

```{python}
#| label: fig-binned-means
#| fig-cap: "Industrial production growth over the next 12 months, averaged within six bins of the term spread. Growth climbs out of inversion and then flattens."
from pathlib import Path

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

DATA = next(p for p in (Path("data"), Path("../data")) if p.exists())
plt.rcParams.update({"figure.figsize": (7, 4.2), "axes.grid": True,
                     "grid.alpha": 0.3, "font.size": 11})

fred = pd.read_parquet(DATA / "fred_macro_monthly.parquet").dropna()
ip_log = np.log(fred["industrial_prod"])
mac = pd.DataFrame({
    "spread": fred["yield_10y"] - fred["fed_funds"],
    "dff": fred["fed_funds"].diff(12),
    "ipg": 100.0 * (ip_log.shift(-12) - ip_log),
}).dropna()

spread_bins = pd.qcut(mac["spread"], 6)
binned = mac.groupby(spread_bins, observed=True)["ipg"].agg(["mean", "count"])

mac_tr = mac.loc[:"1999-12"]
Xd_tr = np.column_stack([np.ones(len(mac_tr)), mac_tr["spread"], mac_tr["dff"]])
b_tr = np.linalg.solve(Xd_tr.T @ Xd_tr, Xd_tr.T @ mac_tr["ipg"].to_numpy())
r2_tr = 1 - np.var(mac_tr["ipg"].to_numpy() - Xd_tr @ b_tr) / np.var(mac_tr["ipg"].to_numpy())

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.4, 4.2))
ax.bar(range(6), binned["mean"], color="steelblue", alpha=0.85)
ax.set_xticks(range(6))
ax.set_xticklabels([f"{iv.left:.1f} to {iv.right:.1f}" for iv in binned.index],
                   fontsize=8, rotation=20)
ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.8)
ax.set_xlabel("term spread, sixth of the sample")
ax.set_ylabel("IP growth over next 12 months, %")
ax.set_title("Growth climbs out of inversion, then stops climbing")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(mac)} months, {mac.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mac.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(binned.round(2))
print(f"linear fit R2, 1961-1999 training window: {r2_tr:.3f}")
```

The binned averages are the shape before any model is fitted. In the lowest sixth of term
spreads, below $-0.42$ points, production over the following year fell by $1.92$ percent
on average. In the next sixth it already grew by $1.36$ percent, and it keeps climbing
through the third and fourth sixths, to $4.12$ and $4.03$. Then it stops: the fifth sixth
gives $2.44$ and the sixth, where spreads exceed $2.51$ points, gives $3.68$. Moving out of
inversion buys six points of growth. Moving from moderately steep to very steep buys
nothing. A straight line fitted through these six points, which is exactly what the linear
regression printed above does, achieves an in-sample $R^2$ of only $0.373$ on the 1961 to
1999 window, and it has to compromise between the steep left-hand part of the picture and
the flat right-hand part, misstating both.

That is the breakdown, and it is the same one Lecture 13 could not see: a model whose
conditional mean is $x^\top\beta$ can only ever draw a straight line through those six
bars, however carefully $\beta$ was estimated or its uncertainty propagated into a
portfolio weight. No earlier chapter assumed the function was straight and got it wrong;
every earlier chapter simply never asked the question, because the question was never
about the functional form. The Minnesota prior of Lecture 6 disciplined a vector of one
hundred and eleven linear coefficients; spike and slab in Lecture 11 disciplined which
linear coefficients were included at all; stochastic volatility in Lecture 12 let a
variance move over time while the conditional mean stayed exactly $x^\top\beta$. Each
repair made the linear model more disciplined without ever asking whether linearity itself
was the constraint that mattered here.

It is worth being precise about what would and would not count as an answer. Adding a
squared term or an interaction to the regression would relax the constraint a little, but
only in the direction chosen in advance, and a macroeconomist rarely knows in advance
whether the true bend is quadratic, logistic, or piecewise flat. What is wanted is a model
that can discover the shape from the data without being told its functional form first,
while still reporting, as every model in this course has, a posterior distribution rather
than a single fitted curve. This chapter asks what happens once a prior is placed on the
function itself rather than on a finite vector of coefficients that presuppose its shape.

## The problem: a linear model is a Gaussian process with one particular kernel {#sec-problem}

### Result R-14.1: linear regression is a Gaussian process, and its kernel is the restriction

Take the Bayesian linear model $y = Xw + \varepsilon$ with $\varepsilon \sim
\mathcal{N}(0,\sigma_n^2 I_n)$ and prior $w \sim \mathcal{N}(0, \sigma_w^2 I_p)$. The
function $f(x) = x^\top w$ is a linear map of a Gaussian vector, hence itself Gaussian,
with mean zero and covariance

$$
\operatorname{Cov}\big(f(x), f(x')\big) = \sigma_w^2\, x^\top x' \equiv k_{\text{lin}}(x,x'),
$$

the linear kernel. Predicting through this covariance, in function space, gives exactly
the ridge or Bayesian linear regression posterior mean computed in weight space; the two
routes describe one model. What the covariance reveals is a restriction rather than an
assumption stated separately: any two inputs that are scalar multiples of one another are
perfectly correlated under $k_{\text{lin}}$, so the posterior mean is confined for every
$n$, $k$ and prior variance to a single hyperplane, $f(x) = x^\top \bar w$ for one fixed
$\bar w$. Nothing in that function class can rise, flatten and stay flat, because a
hyperplane has the same slope everywhere it is evaluated. Linear regression does not merely
happen to draw a straight line here; its assumed covariance permits nothing else.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

In weight space, completing the square exactly as in Lecture 2 gives

$$
w \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar w, \bar\Sigma), \qquad
\bar\Sigma = \Big(\frac{X^\top X}{\sigma_n^2} + \frac{I_p}{\sigma_w^2}\Big)^{-1}, \qquad
\bar w = \big(X^\top X + \lambda I_p\big)^{-1} X^\top y, \qquad \lambda = \frac{\sigma_n^2}{\sigma_w^2},
$$

the ridge estimator with penalty equal to the noise-to-prior variance ratio. In function
space, $K = \sigma_w^2 X X^\top$ and $K_* = \sigma_w^2 X x_*$, and the Gaussian process
posterior mean is $\bar m = K_*^\top(K + \sigma_n^2 I)^{-1} y = \sigma_w^2 x_*^\top
X^\top(\sigma_w^2 XX^\top + \sigma_n^2 I_n)^{-1} y$. The two expressions agree by the
push-through identity $X^\top(XX^\top + \lambda I_n)^{-1} = (X^\top X + \lambda I_p)^{-1}
X^\top$, proved in one line by grouping $X^\top(XX^\top + \lambda I_n) = (X^\top X +
\lambda I_p)X^\top$ two ways and multiplying by the two inverses, both of which exist for
$\lambda > 0$. Substituting $\lambda = \sigma_n^2/\sigma_w^2$ after pulling $\sigma_w^2$ out
of the inverse gives $\bar m = x_*^\top \bar w$ exactly. Replacing $x^\top x'$ by a
different kernel is therefore not a departure from Bayesian regression, it is the same
machine with the covariance term generalised, and the linear kernel is the special case in
which the basis expansion never left the original $p$ coordinates.
:::

The restriction is not only algebra; it can be drawn. A function drawn from a Gaussian
process prior with kernel $k$ is a random curve whose only structure is the one $k$
supplies, so sampling from the prior shows what the model can express before any data are
seen.

```{python}
#| label: fig-kernel-draws
#| fig-cap: "Four draws from the Gaussian process prior over the observed range of the term spread, under a linear kernel and under a squared-exponential kernel."
def sq_exp(xa, xb, ell):
    return np.exp(-0.5 * ((xa[:, None] - xb[None, :]) / ell) ** 2)

def lin_kernel(xa, xb, sw2):
    return sw2 * np.outer(xa, xb)

rng = np.random.default_rng(2026)
grid = np.linspace(mac["spread"].min(), mac["spread"].max(), 200)
K_lin = lin_kernel(grid, grid, 1.0) + 1e-8 * np.eye(len(grid))
K_se = sq_exp(grid, grid, 1.0) + 1e-8 * np.eye(len(grid))
draws_lin = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(len(grid)), K_lin, size=4)
draws_se = rng.multivariate_normal(np.zeros(len(grid)), K_se, size=4)

fig, axes = plt.subplots(1, 2, figsize=(10, 3.8), sharey=True)
for d in draws_lin:
    axes[0].plot(grid, d, lw=1.2)
for d in draws_se:
    axes[1].plot(grid, d, lw=1.2)
axes[0].set_title("Prior draws, linear kernel"); axes[1].set_title("Prior draws, squared-exponential kernel")
for ax in axes:
    ax.set_xlabel("term spread"); ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
axes[0].set_ylabel("f(x)")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

Every draw in the left panel is, and can only be, a straight line through the origin; the
four curves differ only in slope, because $k_{\text{lin}}$ ties $f(x)$ and $f(x')$ together
in exact proportion to $xx'$ and nothing else is available to vary. The right panel, with
the same number of draws from a kernel that measures similarity by distance rather than by
product, produces curves that bend, flatten and reverse direction, because nearby inputs
are tied together without any global straight-line constraint. R-14.1 is the reason for the
difference: a linear model is a Gaussian process, but with the one kernel that rules out
everything the binned means in @sec-motivation showed. The repair is not a different
algorithm, it is a different kernel.

Notice what did not have to change. Nothing about the likelihood, $y = f(x) + \varepsilon$
with Gaussian noise, was touched, and nothing about the logic of conditioning a joint
Normal on observed data was touched either; that machinery is exactly the one used for the
Normal linear model since Lecture 2. What changed is the covariance assigned to the unknown
before any data arrive, from $\sigma_w^2 xx'$ to a function of $\|x - x'\|$ alone. That is
a small edit to write down and a large one in consequence, because it is the covariance,
not the estimation method, that decided in advance that the answer would be a straight
line. The next section states what any such covariance buys once it is allowed to be more
than $k_{\text{lin}}$, and how its own free parameters, the length scale and the noise
variance, get chosen without a validation sample.

## Methodology: a prior over the function, and the evidence that chooses it {#sec-methodology}

A kernel generalises the covariance assignment of R-14.1 to any pair of inputs, subject to
one requirement: it must be positive semidefinite for every finite collection of inputs, so
that any finite set of function values has a valid joint Normal distribution. A Gaussian
process is the statement that all such finite collections are jointly Gaussian under a
chosen $k$. The squared-exponential kernel, $k(x,x') = \sigma_f^2\exp[-\|x - x'\|^2/(2
\ell^2)]$, is the workhorse choice used below: its amplitude $\sigma_f^2$ sets the marginal
variance of the function and its length scale $\ell$ sets the distance over which the
covariance decays, so nearby inputs are treated as similar and distant ones as
uninformative about each other. Writing $f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0,k)$ specifies this prior;
nothing about it names a fixed set of basis functions, and the object being conditioned on
data is a covariance matrix evaluated at the observed and requested inputs, not an explicit
list of coefficients.

### Result R-14.2: the Gaussian process posterior, from one Normal identity

Let $f$ be the latent function at the training inputs $X$ and $f_*$ the latent function at
new inputs $X_*$, with $K = k(X,X)$, $K_* = k(X,X_*)$ and $K_{**} = k(X_*,X_*)$. Under
$f \sim \mathcal{GP}(0,k)$ and $y = f + \varepsilon$, $\varepsilon \sim \mathcal{N}(0,
\sigma_n^2 I_n)$, the joint distribution of data and unknowns is Normal,

$$
\begin{pmatrix} y \\ f_* \end{pmatrix} \sim
\mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \begin{pmatrix} A & K_* \\ K_*^\top & K_{**} \end{pmatrix}\right),
\qquad A = K + \sigma_n^2 I_n,
$$

and conditioning this partitioned Normal on $y$ gives, for any $n$, any number of new
inputs $n_*$ and any positive semidefinite $k$,

$$
f_* \mid y \sim \mathcal{N}(\bar m, \bar V), \qquad
\bar m = K_*^\top A^{-1} y, \qquad
\bar V = K_{**} - K_*^\top A^{-1} K_*.
$$

The posterior mean at a new input is a weighted sum of kernel similarities to the training
inputs with weights $\alpha = A^{-1}y$ that do not depend on the new input at all, so
$\alpha$ is computed once and prediction anywhere costs one further kernel evaluation.
Predicting a realised observation rather than the latent function adds $\sigma_n^2$ to the
diagonal of $\bar V$, because the new observation carries its own fresh shock.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Define the residual $u = f_* - K_*^\top A^{-1} y$. Its covariance with $y$ is
$\operatorname{Cov}(f_*,y) - K_*^\top A^{-1}\operatorname{Cov}(y,y) = K_*^\top -
K_*^\top A^{-1}A = 0$, and for jointly Normal vectors zero covariance is independence, so
$u \perp y$. Since $f_* = K_*^\top A^{-1}y + u$ and $E[u] = 0$,

$$
E[f_* \mid y] = K_*^\top A^{-1} y + E[u \mid y] = K_*^\top A^{-1} y,
$$

which is $\bar m$. Conditioning on $y$ leaves only the randomness in $u$, so
$\operatorname{Var}(f_* \mid y) = \operatorname{Var}(u) = K_{**} - 2K_*^\top A^{-1}K_* +
K_*^\top A^{-1}AA^{-1}K_* = K_{**} - K_*^\top A^{-1}K_*$, which is $\bar V$; notice that $y$
never enters this expression, so the posterior variance depends on where the training
inputs are, not on what was observed there. In practice $A^{-1}$ is never formed. Factor
$A = LL^\top$ by Cholesky, solve $Lz = y$ then $L^\top\alpha = z$ by two triangular solves,
and set $V = L^{-1}K_*$ by one more; then $\bar m = K_*^\top\alpha$ and $\bar V = K_{**} -
V^\top V$.
:::

### Result R-14.3: the marginal likelihood trades fit against complexity

Integrating the latent function out of the model rather than estimating it, the
observations are marginally Normal, $y \sim \mathcal{N}(0,A)$ with $A = K + \sigma_n^2 I$,
and its log density decomposes as

$$
\log p(y \mid X,\theta) = \underbrace{-\tfrac12 y^\top A^{-1}y}_{\text{data fit}}
\;\underbrace{-\;\tfrac12\log|A|}_{\text{complexity penalty}}
\;\underbrace{-\;\tfrac{n}{2}\log 2\pi}_{\text{constant}},
$$

for hyperparameters $\theta$ such as the length scale and noise variance. This quantity, and
not the in-sample fit alone, is what chooses $\theta$: it rewards a covariance that
explains the data and penalises a covariance that could have explained too much else.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true"}
## Derivation

Diagonalise $A = \sum_i \lambda_i u_i u_i^\top$ with orthonormal $u_i$, and write $c_i =
u_i^\top y$. Then $A^{-1} = \sum_i \lambda_i^{-1}u_iu_i^\top$, $|A| = \prod_i\lambda_i$, and
the log density decouples into $n$ one-dimensional problems,
$\log p(y\mid X,\theta) = -\tfrac12\sum_i[c_i^2/\lambda_i + \log\lambda_i] -
\tfrac{n}{2}\log2\pi$. Differentiating the $i$-th term with respect to $\lambda_i$ gives
$-c_i^2/\lambda_i^2 + 1/\lambda_i$, zero and a maximum of the log density at $\lambda_i =
c_i^2$: the marginal likelihood is largest when the model's variance along each direction
matches the squared amount of data observed along it. Too small a $\lambda_i$ makes
$c_i^2/\lambda_i$ explode, the model surprised by data it declared nearly impossible; too
large a $\lambda_i$ makes $\log\lambda_i$ large, the model having spread probability over
outcomes that did not occur, the Occam factor that a fit criterion alone does not have. A
very short length scale makes $K$ nearly diagonal and all eigenvalues small and equal, so
the complexity term is cheap but the smooth component of $y$ falls in the small-eigenvalue
directions and the fit term suffers; a very long length scale makes one eigenvalue of order
$n$ and the rest nearly zero, so one direction is fit beautifully and the model is
astonished by everything else. The interior maximum is the length scale at which the
eigenvalue spectrum of $A$ resembles the spectrum actually present in the data. Two
qualifications matter downstream. The maximisation is over a non-convex surface and can
have several local optima, which is why a grid rather than a gradient step is used below.
And the whole calculation assumes the $n$ observations are conditionally independent given
$f$; when consecutive observations overlap, as a twelve-month-ahead forecast built on
monthly data does, $\log|A|$ counts more independent information than is really there and
the selected $\sigma_n^2$ comes out too small.
:::

R-14.1 fits inside this frame rather than beside it: taking $k = k_{\text{lin}}$ recovers
ridge regression exactly, so the methodology of this section did not abandon the earlier
course, it generalised the one piece, the covariance, that a linear model had fixed in
advance. Everything that follows uses the squared-exponential kernel, one length scale per
predictor, chosen by R-14.3 rather than asserted.

Three practical points follow from R-14.2 and R-14.3 together and are worth stating before
any number appears. First, prediction never requires an explicit basis or an explicit
parameter vector, only the Cholesky factor of an $n \times n$ matrix, so the computational
cost is cubic in the number of training observations regardless of how many predictors
enter the kernel; that is a very different cost profile from a linear model, whose cost is
cubic in the number of predictors and linear in the number of observations, and it is why
a Gaussian process suits a monthly macro panel with a handful of predictors and would not
suit a daily panel with millions of ticks. Second, the same factor $L$ used for the
posterior mean and variance is reused, at no extra cost, to compute the marginal likelihood
of R-14.3, so choosing hyperparameters and predicting from them share almost all of their
arithmetic. Third, R-14.2's posterior variance $\bar V$ does not involve $y$: it depends
only on the kernel evaluated at the training and new inputs. That is a strong and slightly
strange property. It means the width of a Gaussian process's uncertainty band is decided
entirely by where the observations were taken, never by how surprising they turned out to
be, a point the empirical section returns to directly.

With one predictor a single length scale suffices; with several, as in the macro data
below, the natural extension keeps a separate length scale for each coordinate inside the
squared-exponential exponent, $k(x,x') = \sigma_f^2\exp[-\sum_j (x_j - x_j')^2/(2\ell_j^2)]$,
a construction sometimes called automatic relevance determination because a coordinate
whose length scale the evidence pushes very long is, in effect, being told it barely
matters: the kernel becomes nearly constant in that direction and the posterior mean
varies little along it. This is the multivariate counterpart of what the Minnesota prior of
Lecture 6 did with two numbers, $\lambda_1$ and $\lambda_2$, deciding how much of the data's
apparent signal to believe in each direction; there the directions were own lags against
cross lags, here they are the individual predictors, and in both cases the deciding
quantity is chosen by evidence rather than fixed by the modeller.

It is worth being explicit about what R-14.3 does not do. Maximising the marginal
likelihood over $\theta$ is empirical Bayes: a point estimate of the hyperparameters
plugged into R-14.2, not a full posterior over $\theta$ averaged out of the predictive
distribution the way $\sigma^2$ was integrated out of the Normal-Inverse-Gamma regression
of Lecture 2. That approximation is standard practice for Gaussian processes because a
fully Bayesian treatment of the length scale has no closed form and would need the very
sampling machinery Lectures 3 to 5 built; empirical Bayes keeps this chapter's calculation
in closed form at the cost of understating hyperparameter uncertainty, a trade this course
has made before, in the Minnesota prior's own choice of $\lambda_1$ by an out-of-sample
sweep rather than a hierarchical prior over it.

One more comparison is worth making explicit before any data appear, because it sets what
counts as success in @sec-empirical. A Bayesian linear model on the same predictors, of the
kind derived in Lecture 2 and used throughout the middle of this course, is itself the
special case $k = k_{\text{lin}}$ with the noise variance and the prior variance chosen by
the same marginal-likelihood logic; it is not a separate family of methods competing with
Gaussian processes from outside the Bayesian framework, it is the same posterior machinery
evaluated at a covariance R-14.1 already named. That means the empirical comparison below
is not asking whether a Bayesian method beats a non-Bayesian one. It is asking whether
letting the covariance be squared-exponential rather than linear buys anything once both
answers are honestly stated as full predictive distributions, scored the same way, on data
neither model has seen. Framed that way, a negative result is still informative: it says
the extra flexibility purchased nothing once its own uncertainty was accounted for, not
that the Bayesian calculation failed.

## Data: the term spread and industrial production, 1961 to 2025 {#sec-data}

The chapter's dataset is the same monthly FRED macroeconomic snapshot used in
@sec-motivation, `data/fred_macro_monthly.parquet`, restricted to the two predictors and
one outcome already built there: the term spread, the change in the federal funds rate over
the trailing twelve months, and industrial production growth over the following twelve
months. All three are observable at the forecast date except the outcome itself, which is
the object being predicted. No other series is used anywhere in this chapter.

```{python}
#| label: fig-macro-panel-14
#| fig-cap: "The term spread, the funds-rate change and industrial production growth over the next twelve months, monthly."
fig, axes = plt.subplots(3, 1, figsize=(7.4, 6.2), sharex=True)
for ax, col, lab in zip(axes, ["spread", "dff", "ipg"],
                        ["term spread (pts)", "funds-rate change, 12m (pts)",
                         "IP growth, next 12m (%)"]):
    ax.plot(mac.index, mac[col], lw=0.7, color="steelblue")
    ax.axhline(0, color="black", lw=0.6)
    ax.set_ylabel(lab, fontsize=9)
axes[0].set_title("The yield curve, the policy stance, and industrial production growth")
axes[-1].set_xlabel("date")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"{len(mac)} months, {mac.index[0]:%Y-%m} to {mac.index[-1]:%Y-%m}")
print(mac.describe().loc[["mean", "std", "min", "max"]].round(3))
```

The panel runs from January 1961 to June 2025, $774$ months. The term spread averages
$0.986$ points with a standard deviation of $1.618$ and ranges from $-6.51$, the deep
inversion of the early 1980s, to $3.85$. The funds-rate change over a year averages close to
zero, $0.022$, with a standard deviation of $2.108$, and industrial production growth over
the following year averages $2.281$ percent with a standard deviation of $4.705$, its worst
outcome $-19.0$ percent being the year that began in 2020. Every twelve-month window
overlaps the next by eleven months, so consecutive observations are strongly serially
correlated, which the marginal likelihood does not know about and R-14.3's last paragraph
already warned would matter.

The estimation window matters for a Gaussian process in the same way it mattered for the
Minnesota prior of Lecture 6: fitting a single kernel across a sample that runs from the
Volcker disinflation to the post-2020 recovery asks one covariance structure to describe
several different monetary regimes at once. The split used below, training on 1961 to 1999
and testing on 2000 onward, keeps the hyperparameter selection and the honest evaluation on
non-overlapping halves of the sample, and both halves are long enough, $468$ and $306$
months respectively, that the process sees the full range of inversions and expansions in
training before it is asked to forecast any of them.

## Empirical analysis: fitting and testing the process on the yield curve {#sec-empirical}

The kernel is squared-exponential with one length scale per predictor, so the process can
decide separately how quickly the response varies in the spread and in the funds-rate
change. We split at the end of 1999, fit on 1961 to 1999 and keep 2000 onward untouched;
inputs and outcome are standardised on the training sample, and the length scales and noise
variance are chosen by the marginal likelihood of R-14.3 on a grid rather than by
optimisation.

```{python}
def sq_exp_ard(A, B, ell):
    """Squared-exponential kernel with one length scale per input dimension."""
    d = (A[:, None, :] - B[None, :, :]) / ell
    return np.exp(-0.5 * (d ** 2).sum(axis=-1))

def gp_fit_ard(Z, w, ell, sn2):
    """Cholesky factor, alpha, and the log marginal likelihood split into its parts."""
    L = np.linalg.cholesky(sq_exp_ard(Z, Z, ell) + sn2 * np.eye(len(Z)))
    a = np.linalg.solve(L.T, np.linalg.solve(L, w))
    fit = -0.5 * w @ a
    complexity = -np.log(np.diag(L)).sum()
    return L, a, fit + complexity - 0.5 * len(Z) * np.log(2 * np.pi), fit, complexity

def gp_pred_ard(Z, L, a, Zs, ell):
    """Posterior mean and marginal variance of the latent function, R-14.2 in code."""
    Ks = sq_exp_ard(Z, Zs, ell)
    V = np.linalg.solve(L, Ks)
    return Ks.T @ a, np.maximum(1.0 - (V ** 2).sum(axis=0), 0.0)
```

Three functions are the entire algorithm: one kernel evaluation, one Cholesky
factorisation, and two triangular solves, exactly as R-14.2's derivation ends. There is no
optimisation loop inside `gp_fit_ard` itself; choosing the length scales and the noise
variance is a separate step, done next by evaluating the third return value, the marginal
likelihood of R-14.3, over a grid.

```{python}
mac_te = mac.loc["2000-01":]
X_tr = mac_tr[["spread", "dff"]].to_numpy(); y_tr = mac_tr["ipg"].to_numpy()
X_te = mac_te[["spread", "dff"]].to_numpy(); y_te = mac_te["ipg"].to_numpy()
mx, sx = X_tr.mean(axis=0), X_tr.std(axis=0)
my, sy = y_tr.mean(), y_tr.std()
Z_tr, w_tr = (X_tr - mx) / sx, (y_tr - my) / sy
Z_te = (X_te - mx) / sx

cand = [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0]
best = max(((gp_fit_ard(Z_tr, w_tr, np.array([e1, e2]), s)[2], e1, e2, s)
            for e1 in cand for e2 in cand for s in [0.2, 0.4, 0.6, 0.8]))
_, ell1_mac, ell2_mac, sn2_mac = best
ell_mac = np.array([ell1_mac, ell2_mac])
L_mac, a_mac, lml_mac, fit_mac, comp_mac = gp_fit_ard(Z_tr, w_tr, ell_mac, sn2_mac)

print(f"training months {len(mac_tr)}, test months {len(mac_te)}")
print(f"selected length scales: spread {ell1_mac}, funds-rate change {ell2_mac}; "
      f"noise variance {sn2_mac}")
print(f"log marginal likelihood {lml_mac:.2f} = fit {fit_mac:.2f} + "
      f"complexity {comp_mac:.2f} + constant {-0.5*len(Z_tr)*np.log(2*np.pi):.2f}")
```

The marginal likelihood selects a length scale of $0.5$ standardised units in the term
spread and $1.0$ in the funds-rate change, with a noise variance of $0.4$. Half a standard
deviation of the spread is about $0.8$ points, so the process expects the relationship to
bend appreciably over roughly one point of curve slope, close to the scale at which the
binned means of @sec-motivation turned; the funds-rate change is judged twice as smooth,
closer to linear. The decomposition of R-14.3 prints as a fit term of $-220.35$ against a
complexity term of $169.81$, and shortening the length scale moves both, which the next
figure makes explicit before showing what the chosen setting predicts.

```{python}
#| label: fig-gp-curve
#| fig-cap: "The posterior mean and 95% band for industrial production growth against the term spread, at two levels of the funds-rate change, against a linear fit at the mean funds-rate change."
spread_grid = np.linspace(-8.0, 6.0, 200)
q25_dff, q75_dff = np.percentile(X_tr[:, 1], [25, 75])

fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7.6, 4.6))
ax.scatter(X_tr[:, 0], y_tr, s=10, color="grey", alpha=0.45, label="1961-1999 months")
for lev, colour, lbl in [(q25_dff, "C0", f"easing, funds rate {q25_dff:+.1f} pts"),
                         (q75_dff, "C3", f"tightening, funds rate {q75_dff:+.1f} pts")]:
    Zs = np.column_stack([(spread_grid - mx[0]) / sx[0],
                          np.full(200, (lev - mx[1]) / sx[1])])
    m_s, v_s = gp_pred_ard(Z_tr, L_mac, a_mac, Zs, ell_mac)
    m_s, sd_s = m_s * sy + my, np.sqrt(v_s) * sy
    ax.plot(spread_grid, m_s, color=colour, lw=1.9, label=lbl)
    ax.fill_between(spread_grid, m_s - 1.96 * sd_s, m_s + 1.96 * sd_s, color=colour, alpha=0.18)
b_lin_mac = np.linalg.solve(np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_tr)), X_tr]).T
                            @ np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_tr)), X_tr]),
                            np.column_stack([np.ones(len(X_tr)), X_tr]).T @ y_tr)
ax.plot(spread_grid, b_lin_mac[0] + b_lin_mac[1] * spread_grid,
        color="black", ls="--", lw=1.4, label="linear fit, mean funds-rate change")
ax.axvspan(X_tr[:, 0].min(), X_tr[:, 0].max(), color="C2", alpha=0.05)
ax.set_xlabel("term spread, points"); ax.set_ylabel("IP growth over next 12 months, %")
ax.set_title("The yield curve signal bends, and the band flares where no data lie")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, loc="lower right")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

for lev, lbl in [(q25_dff, "easing"), (q75_dff, "tightening")]:
    Zs = np.column_stack([(spread_grid - mx[0]) / sx[0],
                          np.full(200, (lev - mx[1]) / sx[1])])
    m_s, v_s = gp_pred_ard(Z_tr, L_mac, a_mac, Zs, ell_mac)
    m_s, sd_s = m_s * sy + my, np.sqrt(v_s) * sy
    picks = {q: (round(float(m_s[np.argmin(abs(spread_grid - q))]), 2),
                 round(float(sd_s[np.argmin(abs(spread_grid - q))]), 2))
             for q in [-7, -4, -2, 0, 1, 2, 3, 5]}
    print(lbl, "mean and sd at selected spreads:", picks)
print(f"training spread range: {X_tr[:, 0].min():.2f} to {X_tr[:, 0].max():.2f}")
```

The figure carries two messages. The first is the shape itself: along the tightening curve
a spread of $-2$ implies growth of $-6.11$ percent, climbing steeply to $4.96$ at a spread
of one and then flattening, $2.56$ at two and $4.16$ at three, while the dashed linear fit
runs through the middle of both the steep part and the flat part and misstates each. The
second is the interaction the two predictors carry together: deep in inversion the
tightening curve sits far below the easing one, $-8.80$ against $-2.57$ at a spread of
$-4$, so a curve inverted because policy has been raised hard is a worse signal than a
curve inverted with policy unchanged, and the two curves converge once the spread turns
positive. That is a genuine two-dimensional non-linearity invisible to any model that adds
the two predictors rather than lets them interact through a shared kernel.

Notice too what the shaded region in the figure is doing. Inside it, where the training
spreads actually lie, the bands for both scenarios are visibly narrow; the picture does not
show it directly, but the numbers behind it do, a posterior standard deviation under half a
percent near the middle of the training range against several points once the grid runs
past $-6.5$ or $3.85$, the observed extremes. That flaring is not a modelling choice, it is
what R-14.2 requires: the posterior variance depends only on distance to the training
inputs, so a region with no training data anywhere near it must inherit variance close to
the prior's, regardless of how confidently the curve is drawn where data are dense. A
polynomial regression fitted to the same points would extrapolate past $-6.5$ with the same
confidence it has at the centre of the sample, which is precisely the failure mode R-14.1
already diagnosed: a fixed functional form carries its assumptions into regions no
observation has tested.

The choice of length scale is not free of consequence, and the next check is whether the
value R-14.3 picked is also the value that forecasts best, which are two different
questions answered by two different criteria.

```{python}
#| label: fig-length-scale-sweep
#| fig-cap: "Log marginal likelihood and out-of-sample RMSE as the length scale on the term spread varies, holding the funds-rate length scale and noise variance fixed at their selected values."
ell1_try = [0.15, 0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0, 4.0, 8.0]
sweep_rows = []
for e1 in ell1_try:
    ell_t = np.array([e1, ell2_mac])
    Lt, at, lml_t, fit_t, comp_t = gp_fit_ard(Z_tr, w_tr, ell_t, sn2_mac)
    m_out, _ = gp_pred_ard(Z_tr, Lt, at, Z_te, ell_t)
    sweep_rows.append({"length scale": e1, "log marg lik": lml_t, "fit term": fit_t,
                       "complexity term": comp_t,
                       "out-of-sample RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((y_te - (m_out * sy + my)) ** 2))})
sweep = pd.DataFrame(sweep_rows).set_index("length scale")
print(sweep.round(3).to_string())

fig, ax1 = plt.subplots()
ax1.plot(sweep.index, sweep["log marg lik"], "o-", color="C0", label="log marginal likelihood")
ax1.set_xscale("log"); ax1.set_xlabel("length scale on the term spread (log scale)")
ax1.set_ylabel("log marginal likelihood", color="C0"); ax1.axvline(ell1_mac, color="C0", ls=":", lw=1.2)
ax2 = ax1.twinx()
ax2.plot(sweep.index, sweep["out-of-sample RMSE"], "s--", color="C3", label="out-of-sample RMSE")
ax2.set_ylabel("out-of-sample RMSE, %", color="C3"); ax2.grid(False)
ax1.set_title("An interior maximum the test error barely notices")
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()
```

The left-hand axis is R-14.3 in a picture. Shrinking the length scale from $0.5$ to $0.15$
raises the fit term from $-220.35$ to $-211.19$ but costs $36.7$ in the complexity term,
and the marginal likelihood falls; stretching it to $8.0$ loses fit faster than it saves in
complexity. The maximum at $0.5$ is interior and comes from the training data and the prior
alone. The right-hand axis is the deflating half: out-of-sample RMSE over 2000 to 2025
moves only from $6.02$ to $6.17$ across the whole grid, and its minimum is not exactly at
the value the evidence chose. The curvature the process found is real and was found by a
principled route, and it makes little difference to how well the model forecasts, a pattern
worth expecting rather than resenting. It is also the practical answer to a question a
sceptical student should ask before trusting any of this: could the same shape have been
manufactured by an unlucky choice of hyperparameter? The table shows that every setting on
the grid, from a length scale six times shorter than the selected one to sixteen times
longer, agrees to within a percentage point of predicted growth on out-of-sample error, so
the shape in @fig-gp-curve is not an artefact of the particular length scale R-14.3
happened to prefer.

The forecasting question needs its own test, because coefficients and curves are not the
object of interest. We run an expanding-window comparison from January 1990, refitting
every three months on all twelve-month windows that have already closed, forecasting the
next month, and scoring the Gaussian process against a Bayesian linear model on the same
two predictors and the historical mean of the training window, a forecast that ignores the
yield curve entirely.

```{python}
from scipy import stats

X_all = mac[["spread", "dff"]].to_numpy(); y_all = mac["ipg"].to_numpy(); idx_all = mac.index
h_mac, t_start = 12, int(np.searchsorted(idx_all, pd.Timestamp("1990-01-01")))
hyp_grid = [(e1, e2, s) for e1 in [0.25, 0.5, 1.0, 2.0]
            for e2 in [0.5, 1.0, 2.0] for s in [0.3, 0.4, 0.6]]

oos_rows, hyp_sel, cache = [], None, None
for t in range(t_start, len(y_all)):
    if (t - t_start) % 3 == 0:
        end = t - h_mac
        Xs, ys = X_all[:end], y_all[:end]
        mxs, sxs = Xs.mean(axis=0), Xs.std(axis=0)
        mys, sys_ = ys.mean(), ys.std()
        Zs, ws = (Xs - mxs) / sxs, (ys - mys) / sys_
        if hyp_sel is None:
            hyp_sel = max(hyp_grid, key=lambda g: gp_fit_ard(Zs, ws, np.array(g[:2]), g[2])[2])
        e_sel, sn_sel = np.array(hyp_sel[:2]), hyp_sel[2]
        Lc, ac = gp_fit_ard(Zs, ws, e_sel, sn_sel)[:2]
        Xd = np.column_stack([np.ones(end), Xs])
        bb = np.linalg.solve(Xd.T @ Xd, Xd.T @ ys)
        ee = ys - Xd @ bb
        dof = end - 3
        s2 = ee @ ee / dof
        XtXi = np.linalg.inv(Xd.T @ Xd)
        cache = (mxs, sxs, mys, sys_, Zs, Lc, ac, e_sel, sn_sel, bb, s2, XtXi, dof,
                 ys.mean(), ys.std())
    (mxs, sxs, mys, sys_, Zs, Lc, ac, e_sel, sn_sel, bb, s2, XtXi, dof,
     hist_m, hist_s) = cache
    m_g, v_g = gp_pred_ard(Zs, Lc, ac, (X_all[t:t + 1] - mxs) / sxs, e_sel)
    xo = np.r_[1.0, X_all[t]]
    oos_rows.append((idx_all[t], X_all[t, 0], y_all[t],
                     m_g[0] * sys_ + mys, np.sqrt(v_g[0] + sn_sel) * sys_,
                     float(xo @ bb), float(np.sqrt(s2 * (1 + xo @ XtXi @ xo))),
                     dof, hist_m, hist_s))

oos = pd.DataFrame(oos_rows, columns=["date", "spread", "y", "gp_m", "gp_sd",
                                      "lin_m", "lin_sd", "dof", "hist_m", "hist_sd"]).set_index("date")

def score_block(sub, label):
    return {"regime": label, "months": len(sub),
            "GP RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((sub.y - sub.gp_m) ** 2)),
            "linear RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((sub.y - sub.lin_m) ** 2)),
            "mean RMSE": np.sqrt(np.mean((sub.y - sub.hist_m) ** 2)),
            "GP log score": np.mean(stats.norm.logpdf(sub.y, sub.gp_m, sub.gp_sd)),
            "linear log score": np.mean(stats.t.logpdf((sub.y - sub.lin_m) / sub.lin_sd,
                                                       df=sub.dof) - np.log(sub.lin_sd)),
            "mean log score": np.mean(stats.norm.logpdf(sub.y, sub.hist_m, sub.hist_sd))}

blocks = [score_block(oos, "all months"), score_block(oos[oos.spread < 0], "inverted"),
          score_block(oos[(oos.spread >= 0) & (oos.spread < 1.5)], "flat"),
          score_block(oos[oos.spread >= 1.5], "steep")]
print(pd.DataFrame(blocks).set_index("regime").round(3).T)
```

Over all $426$ months from 1990 to 2025, the Gaussian process has a root mean squared error
of $5.05$, the linear model $4.89$, and the historical mean $4.51$: neither model beats
ignoring the yield curve, because output growth trended down across the sample and both
models carry a stale intercept through 2008 and 2020, shocks no term spread foreshadowed.
Split by regime the picture matches the economics. In the $71$ inverted months both models
beat the historical mean by roughly a sixth, $4.94$ and $4.87$ against $5.84$; in the $202$
steep months the mean wins comfortably, $3.67$ against $4.53$ and $4.96$, because a steep
curve says only "conditions are normal" and the models insist on using it anyway. The
remaining $153$ flat months, spreads between zero and $1.5$ points, sit in between, all
three forecasts clustering near five percent RMSE, which is exactly the region of
@fig-gp-curve where the tightening and easing curves have not yet separated and the term
spread is telling the models the least. The value of the whole exercise is therefore
concentrated in under a fifth of the sample, the months an inversion is actually under way,
which a single overall RMSE hides and the regime split reveals.

The log scores tell a harsher story: the process scores $-3.81$ against the linear model's
$-3.12$ and the mean's $-2.97$, a far larger gap than the RMSE numbers suggest, and
R-14.3's last warning is why: the $468$ overlapping training months carry closer to forty
independent observations, and a marginal likelihood that treats them as independent selects
a noise variance too small, producing bands so narrow that a miss is punished heavily.
Non-linearity pays at turning points and nowhere else in this dataset, and a marginal
likelihood computed under an assumption the data violate will select an overconfident
model, a fact the log score reveals and the squared error does not. A practitioner who
read only the RMSE row of the table above would conclude the Gaussian process is a mild
disappointment; one who also read the log score would conclude its stated uncertainty
cannot be trusted at face value, which is the sharper and more useful warning of the two.

```{python}
#| label: fig-oos-timeseries
#| fig-cap: "Gaussian process and linear forecasts against realised twelve-month industrial production growth, 1990 to 2025."
fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(8, 4.4))
ax.fill_between(oos.index, oos.gp_m - 1.96 * oos.gp_sd, oos.gp_m + 1.96 * oos.gp_sd,
                color="C0", alpha=0.2, label="GP 95% predictive band")
ax.plot(oos.index, oos.gp_m, color="C0", lw=1.2, label="GP forecast")
ax.plot(oos.index, oos.lin_m, color="C3", lw=1.0, label="linear forecast")
ax.plot(oos.index, oos.y, color="black", lw=1.3, label="realised growth")
ax.axhline(0, color="grey", lw=0.7, ls=":")
ax.set_xlabel("forecast date"); ax.set_ylabel("IP growth over next 12 months, %")
ax.set_title("Both forecasts are flat next to the shocks they never saw coming")
ax.legend(fontsize=8, ncol=2)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

worst = oos.assign(err=(oos.y - oos.gp_m).abs()).nlargest(3, "err")
print(worst[["y", "gp_m", "gp_sd", "lin_m"]].round(2))
```

Both forecast lines sit close to their long-run averages next to a realised series that
swings from about $+15$ percent in the 2021 rebound to $-19$ and $-16$ in the years that
began in 2019 and 2008. Those three dates are the three largest errors either model makes,
and the predictive band drawn around the Gaussian process forecast does not come close to
covering any of them, which is the practical face of the log-score gap already reported: a
band that is honest about distance from training inputs is not thereby honest about a
pandemic or a banking crisis, because neither event is encoded in the term spread or the
funds rate at all. What the line does show is a forecast that moves in a useful direction
some of the time, dipping ahead of the two recessions that followed an inversion and
sitting close to its unconditional level otherwise, which is the regime-split result of the
previous table drawn as a single picture instead of a table.

## Discussion: an honest band is not the same as a useful one {#sec-discussion}

The yield curve's non-linearity is real: the binned means of @sec-motivation showed a
shape no coefficient can draw, R-14.1 explained why a linear model cannot draw it, and the
posterior mean of @sec-empirical drew it, steep out of inversion and flat beyond. What that
shape buys in forecasting is concentrated in the $71$ months when the curve is actually
inverted, and is absent, even negative, everywhere else, which is the sense in which the
answer is smaller than the shape suggests. Flexibility recovered a shape that was really
there; it did not, on this dataset, turn that shape into a forecast that beats simply
reporting the training-window average across the whole sample, and separating those two
claims is the chapter's central discipline. A referee who only asked "is the relationship
non-linear" would have been answered yes and would have stopped looking; a referee who
asked "does the non-linear model forecast better" needed the regime split and the log score
to find out that the honest answer is only sometimes, and by an amount too small to read
off the curve in @fig-gp-curve.

R-14.2 makes a specific, checkable claim: the posterior variance $\bar V$ does not depend
on $y$ at all, only on where the training and new inputs sit relative to one another. That
is worth checking directly rather than taking on faith, since it is the property that makes
a Gaussian process say "I do not know" honestly rather than merely report a residual
standard deviation.

```{python}
#| label: fig-honest-bands
#| fig-cap: "Posterior standard deviation of the funds-rate-13 model at the tightening scenario, as a function of distance from the training range of the term spread."
Zs_check = np.column_stack([(spread_grid - mx[0]) / sx[0],
                            np.full(200, (q75_dff - mx[1]) / sx[1])])
_, v_check = gp_pred_ard(Z_tr, L_mac, a_mac, Zs_check, ell_mac)
sd_check = np.sqrt(v_check) * sy

fig, ax = plt.subplots()
ax.plot(spread_grid, sd_check, color="C3", lw=1.8)
ax.axvspan(X_tr[:, 0].min(), X_tr[:, 0].max(), color="C2", alpha=0.08, label="training range")
ax.set_xlabel("term spread, points"); ax.set_ylabel("posterior sd of the latent function, %")
ax.set_title("The band widens with distance from the data, not with any observed value")
ax.legend(fontsize=9)
plt.tight_layout(); plt.show()

print(f"posterior sd at spread=1 (inside range): {sd_check[np.argmin(abs(spread_grid-1))]:.2f}")
print(f"posterior sd at spread=-7 (outside range): {sd_check[np.argmin(abs(spread_grid-(-7)))]:.2f}")
```

Inside the shaded training range the band sits near its narrowest, a posterior standard
deviation of about half a percentage point where hundreds of months cluster; a few points
beyond either edge it climbs past four, an eightfold increase driven entirely by distance
from the training inputs, exactly as R-14.2's derivation said it must be, since $y$ never
enters $\bar V$. A cubic polynomial fitted to the same data would extrapolate into that
region with total confidence and, on this dataset, a large error, since the deepest
inversion in the record already sits close to the edge of what the model has seen.

The check against something already known is R-14.2's own claim that $\bar V$ ignores $y$.
That is not a property special to macro data or to this kernel; it follows from the
partitioned Normal identity in exactly the way the Kalman filter's state uncertainty in
Lecture 8 follows from a different partitioned Normal identity, and in exactly the way the
shrinkage matrix of Lecture 6 depended on the design and the prior but never on the
realised $y$. Wherever this course has produced a closed-form Gaussian posterior, the
spread of that posterior has been a statement about the experiment, not about the outcome,
and the figure above is that statement made visible for a model whose parameter is an
entire function rather than a finite vector.

The limitation is the one the log score exposed and it does not go away with more data of
the same kind. A twelve-month-ahead design manufactures serial correlation that a marginal
likelihood does not model, so the noise variance it selects is too small and the resulting
band, honestly shaped as R-14.2 requires, is nonetheless too narrow in absolute terms.
Fixing that needs the state-space and stochastic-volatility machinery of Lectures 8 and 12
applied to the noise process itself, which this chapter has not done, and it needs a
likelihood built for overlapping data, which none of this course's closed-form results
supply out of the box. Lecture 15 is the last of the course and draws every piece built so
far, this one included, into a single retelling on one dataset, closing the chain rather
than opening a new link in it.

## Exercises

These are the chapter's practice questions; the [Week 14 exercise
session](../exercise-sessions/14-bayesian-machine-learning.qmd) works through them and adds
the lab.

1. By hand. Starting from R-14.1, show what happens to the ridge estimator $\bar w =
   (X^\top X + \lambda I_p)^{-1}X^\top y$ as $\sigma_w^2 \to \infty$ with $\sigma_n^2$
   fixed, and confirm the Gaussian process posterior mean under the linear kernel converges
   to the same limit as $\sigma_w^2 \to \infty$. Then show that at $\sigma_w^2 = \infty$
   the linear kernel posterior mean is exactly the least-squares fit, so R-14.1 recovers
   the very method it diagnoses at one extreme of the prior.

2. Computational. The tree ensemble that this course's chain lists alongside the Gaussian
   process, BART, places a different kind of prior over functions: a sum of shallow
   regression trees, each shrunk toward zero at the leaf. Build one tree from scratch by
   the recipe in the exercise materials, apply the leaf-posterior-mean formula given there
   with a chosen prior variance, and compare its marginal likelihood behaviour to the
   length-scale sweep of @sec-empirical: does adding more trees, like shortening the length
   scale, trade fit for complexity in the same qualitative way?

3. On real data. The exercise materials set up a second horse race, a Bayesian linear
   model against the BART-style ensemble of question 2, on the forty-nine Fama-French
   industry portfolios rather than the macro panel of this chapter. Run it, report the
   out-of-sample root mean squared error and log predictive score of both models against a
   historical-mean benchmark, and explain, using R-14.3's warning about complexity, why a
   flexible model can lose to a linear one on this second dataset even though it won
   convincingly on the first.

Exercise 1 is the one to attempt before the session, since it is the algebra behind R-14.1
restated as a limit. Exercises 2 and 3 are written for the session itself.

## Reading and references {#sec-reading}

The Gaussian process construction, R-14.2 and its Cholesky-based implementation follow
Rasmussen and Williams (2006), Chapter 2, which is also the source for the automatic
relevance determination kernel used in @sec-empirical. The marginal likelihood
decomposition of R-14.3 and its interpretation as an Occam factor follow the same source,
Chapter 5, and the same chapter is the reference for the practical warning about
non-independent observations used in the discussion above. The ridge-as-Gaussian-process
argument behind R-14.1 is standard and appears in the same reference alongside the
basis-function view of kernel regression more generally, connecting this lecture back to
the Normal linear model of Lecture 2 rather than presenting Gaussian processes as an
unrelated idea. The tree-ensemble prior used in the exercise session, BART, is Chipman,
George and McCulloch (2010), and the infinite-width equivalence between Bayesian neural
networks and Gaussian processes mentioned in the exercise materials is Neal (1996), the
result that keeps the exercise session's second flexible method inside the same family as
the one derived here rather than treating it as a competitor from outside Bayesian
statistics.

The explanations and exercises are adapted to this course's notation and weekly
structure; consult the cited originals for the full treatments.

Chipman, George and McCulloch, *BART: Bayesian Additive Regression Trees*, Ann. Appl.
